title: Load Shedding & Overload Control
summary: When load exceeds capacity, systems must shed work intentionally — or they shed it randomly via timeouts and cascading failure. Good overload control protects latency for admitted traffic.

sections.title: Failure mode of uncontrolled overload
paragraphs: Queues grow, latency explodes, retries amplify load, thread pools saturate, and the service spends CPU on work that will be cancelled. Success rate collapses.

sections.title: Shedding strategies
paragraphs: Admit based on queue time, concurrency, or token buckets. Prefer shedding new low-priority work. Return explicit 503 with Retry-After.
Codel/adaptive LIFO approaches protect latency better than unbounded FIFO under overload.

sections.title: Client cooperation
paragraphs: Clients must backoff. Without coordinated retry budgets, shedding just moves the thundering herd.

sections.title: Place in the stack
paragraphs: Shed at edges and at each dependency boundary. Bulkheads prevent one capability from consuming all workers.

deepDive.title: Load Shedding & Overload Control — Operations
paragraphs: Operating Load Shedding & Overload Control in production means defining SLIs before tuning knobs, knowing amplification costs, and rehearsing failure modes.
Prefer reversible changes, feature flags, and canaries. Measure p50/p99 and error rate under load that matches production skew.
bullets: Define capacity from the scarcest resource
Keep rollback cheaper than forward repair when possible

deepDive.title: Load Shedding & Overload Control — Failure modes
paragraphs: Common failures around Load Shedding & Overload Control include overload, partial dependency outages, and silent correctness bugs that pass happy-path tests.
Inject faults in staging: latency, loss, clock skew, and disk full. Verify alerts fire and degradation is intentional.

expert.title: Load Shedding & Overload Control — Expert notes
paragraphs: At the expert level, Load Shedding & Overload Control intersects multi-region consistency, cost envelopes, and organizational constraints (team ownership, on-call load).
Write down the non-goals. Many outages come from optimizing a metric that was never the product requirement.

whyItMatters: Most cascading outages are overload without admission control.
reflectionQuestions: What work can you drop first under overload?
numbersToKnow: Know your p99 latency budget before adding hops
Peak load ≠ average load — plan headroom (often 2–3×)
Cross-region RTT is often ~50–150ms one way
